info.headline: Read short sentences with pictures, charts, and tables.
info.summary: Starting readers work with 2–4 short sentences about familiar topics like school, home, plants, and animals. I can put pictures and sentences in order.

activities.title: Amara's Garden
activities.skill: Finding a key detail with a picture
activities.directions: Look at the picture. Read the sentences. Choose the best answer.
activities.prompt: What does Amara water?
passage: Amara works in the school garden.
She waters the tomatoes with a green watering can.
The sunflowers are taller than Amara!

picture.alt: A girl pours water from a green watering can onto red tomato plants in a school garden. Tall yellow sunflowers grow next to her.

vocabulary: garden
a place where people grow plants
jardín: un lugar donde se cultivan plantas
water
to give water to a plant
regar: darle agua a una planta
tall
high from the bottom to the top
alto: que mide mucho de abajo hacia arriba
readFor: the name of a plant after it
activities.correct: Yes! The text says she waters the tomatoes, and the picture shows water falling on the red tomatoes.
activities.hint: Find the word waters in sentence 2. Read the next word.
activities.support: Point to each plant in the picture and say its name: tomatoes, sunflowers. Then find those words in the text.
activities.extension: Write one more sentence about the garden. Start with: The sunflowers are ___.

teacher.use: Warm-up for 'right there' detail questions with picture support.
teacher.function: Locating a key detail; matching a noun to an image.
teacher.lower: Read the sentences aloud and point to each plant as you name it.
teacher.onLevel: Students read independently and find the word that follows waters.
teacher.challenge: Students tell what Amara might do next in the garden.
teacher.noTech: Print the picture and text; students circle the plant Amara waters.
teacher.prompt: What would you grow in a school garden?

activities.title: From Egg to Frog
activities.skill: Putting events in order
activities.directions: Look at the picture of the frog's life. Read the sentences. Put the steps in order.
activities.prompt: Put the frog's life steps in order. Start with the first step.
passage: A frog starts life as a tiny egg in a pond.
The egg hatches into a tadpole with a long tail.
The tadpole grows four legs.
At last, it is a frog that can hop on land.

picture.alt: Four stages of a frog's life in a circle with arrows: frog eggs in water, a tadpole with a long tail, a tadpole with four legs, and a grown frog.

items.text: The tadpole grows four legs.
A frog starts as a tiny egg.
It is a frog that can hop on land.
The egg hatches into a tadpole.

vocabulary: egg
a small round thing a baby animal comes out of
huevo: cosa redonda de donde sale un animal bebé
tadpole
a baby frog that swims and has a tail
renacuajo: una rana bebé que nada y tiene cola
hatch
to come out of an egg
salir del huevo (eclosionar): cuando un animal sale del huevo
readFor: order words like starts and at last
what the frog looks like at each step
activities.correct: Great ordering! Egg, then tadpole, then a tadpole with legs, then a frog. The words starts and at last are clues.
activities.hint: Which sentence has the word starts? That is the first step. Which has at last?
activities.support: Follow the arrows in the picture with your finger. Say: egg, tadpole, legs, frog.
activities.extension: Tell the steps to a partner using first, next, then, and last.

teacher.use: Sequencing routine with a science life cycle (Grade 3 life science).
teacher.function: Ordering events; noticing signal words (starts, at last).
teacher.lower: Act out each stage with hands (small egg, wiggly tail, legs, hop).
teacher.onLevel: Students order the sentences independently and read them aloud.
teacher.challenge: Students compare the frog cycle to a butterfly's life cycle.
teacher.noTech: Cut the four sentences into strips; students order them on a desk.
teacher.prompt: What other animals change as they grow?

activities.title: Recycling Day

activities.directions: Look at the picture. Read the sentences. Sort each thing into the right bin.

activities.title: Parts of a Plant

teacher.onLevel: Students match each label to a sentence in the text.

activities.title: A Rainy Morning

B.studentGoal: I can read a short passage and use details, order words, and graphs to answer questions.

info.headline: Read short passages, letters, poems, and how-to texts.
info.summary: Growing readers read passages of about 80–140 words: science and social studies articles, stories, a friendly letter, a how-to text, and a poem. I can explain cause and effect with because.
I can use a graph or table with a text to answer questions.

activities.title: The Lemonade Stand
activities.skill: Using a table to solve a word problem
activities.directions: Read the story. Look at the picture and the table. Then choose the best answer.
activities.prompt: How many cups of lemonade did Zainab and Omar sell in all on Saturday and Sunday?
passage: Zainab and her brother Omar want to help pay for their class trip to the aquarium. They decide to sell lemonade in front of their apartment building. Their mom helps them make two big pitchers, and Omar paints a colorful sign.

On Saturday, the sun is hot, and many neighbors stop to buy a cup. Each cup costs 50 cents. On Sunday, it is even hotter, so they sell more cups. Zainab writes the number of cups they sell each day in a table so they can count their money at the end.

vocabulary: pitcher
a large container with a handle for pouring drinks

neighbor

vecino: una persona que vive cerca de ti
in all

en total: todo junto; sumar los números
frames: They sold ___ cups on Saturday and ___ cups on Sunday.
activities.correct: Correct! 12 cups on Saturday + 18 cups on Sunday = 30 cups in all.

activities.support: 12 is only Saturday and 18 is only Sunday. Add them: 12 + 18 = ?
activities.extension: Each cup costs 50 cents. How much money did they make on Saturday? (Hint: 2 cups = $1.)

teacher.function: Reading a table; recognizing the key phrase in all as addition.

teacher.onLevel: Students solve and explain using the frames.
teacher.challenge: Students find the money earned each day (12 × $0.50, 18 × $0.50).

teacher.prompt: How could your class raise money for a trip?

activities.title: A Letter to Abuela
activities.skill: Finding the author's purpose in a letter
activities.directions: Read Mateo's letter. Then click the sentence that answers the question.
activities.prompt: Why did Mateo write this letter? Click the sentence that tells his MAIN reason.

sentences.text: Dear Abuela, I hope you are well in Guatemala.
Yesterday was a very special day for me.
When I woke up, everything outside was white because it snowed for the first time this winter!
My friend Dami and I built a snowman in the park next to our school.
I wore the warm blue scarf that you knitted for me, and my neck stayed toasty the whole time.
I am writing to say thank you for that wonderful gift.
Mamá says we can visit you in the summer, and I will bring photos of our snowman.

activities.hint: Look for the words I am writing to. They often tell the purpose of a letter.
activities.support: The snow and the snowman are details. Which sentence tells what Mateo wants to SAY to Abuela?
activities.extension: Write a two-sentence thank-you note to someone who helped you.

teacher.onLevel: Students click the purpose sentence and name one supporting detail.

activities.title: How to Plant a Bean Seed
activities.skill: Ordering steps in a procedure
activities.directions: Read the how-to text. Then put the steps in the correct order.
activities.prompt: Put the steps for planting a bean seed in order.
activities.passageTitle: How to Plant a Bean Seed
passage: Do you want to watch a plant grow? You can plant a bean seed in a cup at school or at home.

First, poke a few small holes in the bottom of a paper cup so extra water can drain out. Next, fill the cup with soil almost to the top. Then, push the bean seed into the soil about as deep as the first part of your finger. After that, water the soil until it is damp but not muddy. Finally, put the cup on a sunny windowsill. In about one week, a tiny green sprout will push up through the soil.

items.text: Water the soil until it is damp.
Poke small holes in the bottom of the cup.
Put the cup on a sunny windowsill.
Fill the cup with soil.
Push the bean seed into the soil.

to let water flow out
drenar (escurrir): dejar que salga el agua

brote: una planta nueva y pequeña que empieza a crecer
readFor: order words: first, next, then, after that, finally

activities.correct: Well done! The order words first, next, then, after that, and finally show the steps.
activities.hint: Find the word First in the text. Then look for Next, Then, After that, and Finally.
activities.support: Circle the five order words. The sentence after each one is a step.
activities.extension: Why do you poke holes in the cup? Find the reason in the text.

teacher.use: Procedural text routine (how-to), connects to Grade 3 plant life cycles.
teacher.function: Tracking transition words to sequence steps.
teacher.lower: Do the steps with a real cup and seed while reading aloud.
teacher.onLevel: Students order the steps and retell them to a partner.

activities.skill: Sequencing a process with headings and a diagram

passage: The water on Earth is always moving. The same water has been used again and again for millions of years. Its journey from the ground to the sky and back again is called the water cycle.
Evaporation: When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of the water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor. The vapor rises up into the air.
Condensation: High in the sky, the air is cooler. The water vapor cools down and turns back into tiny drops of water. Millions of these drops join together to form clouds.
Precipitation: When the drops in a cloud get too big and heavy, they fall to the ground. This is called precipitation. It can be rain, snow, sleet, or hail, depending on how cold the air is.
Collection: The water collects in oceans, lakes, and rivers, or it soaks into the ground. Then the sun heats it again, and the cycle starts all over.

sentences.text: Ellen Ochoa grew up in La Mesa, California, with her mother and four brothers and sisters.
Her mother took college classes for many years while raising her children, and she taught Ellen that learning is important.

Ellen applied to become an astronaut, but NASA did not choose her the first time.
She did not give up; she kept working hard, earned her pilot's license, and applied again.
In 1990, NASA selected her, and in 1993 she became the first Hispanic woman to travel to space.
She even brought her flute on the space shuttle and played it while orbiting Earth.

The Sonoran Desert stretches across parts of Arizona, California, and Mexico. It gets very little rain, usually less than 12 inches in a whole year. Monkeys, parrots, and sloths live high in the trees, where they find fruit and leaves to eat.

passage: What Is a Volcano? A volcano is an opening in Earth's surface where melted rock, gas, and ash can escape. Deep underground, it is so hot that some rock melts. This melted rock is called magma.

How Does a Volcano Erupt? Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. It collects in a space called a magma chamber. When too much pressure builds up, the magma bursts through cracks to the surface. Once magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. Over many eruptions, layers of cooled lava and ash pile up and build a mountain.

Are Volcanoes Helpful? Volcanoes can be dangerous, but they also help people. Ash from old eruptions breaks down into rich soil that is good for growing crops. In Iceland, people use heat from deep underground near volcanoes to warm their homes and make electricity.
Fact box — Did you know? All of the Hawaiian Islands were made by volcanoes rising from the ocean floor.
